title: Judges 16:4–14
context: Samson loves Delilah, a woman in the valley of Sorek. The Philistine lords offer her a large bribe to discover the secret of his strength. Three times she asks, three times Samson gives a false answer, and three times she tests it with the Philistines hidden nearby. The episode shows a man toying with danger, a woman willing to sell him, and the slow erosion of Samson's guard.

verses.text: It came to pass afterward that he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.
verses.arminianNotes: Samson "loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah." Her nationality is not stated. Arminian readers note this is the only woman in Samson's story who is named, and the first time the narrator says Samson loved anyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson's affections, never governed by his calling, now lead to his ruin. The text does not say Delilah was a Philistine, but her loyalty proves to lie with them, not with him.

verses.text: The lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, “Entice him, and see in which his great strength lies, and by what means we may prevail against him, that we may bind him to afflict him; and we will each give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”
verses.arminianNotes: The lords offer "eleven hundred pieces of silver" each to learn how to "afflict" him. Arminian readers see the moral weight of Delilah's choice: she is offered money to betray, and she freely accepts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the size of the bribe as a measure of how much the Philistines feared Samson. Delilah's greed and the lords' scheming are real sins, even as God will use the whole affair for his purposes.

verses.text: Delilah said to Samson, “Please tell me where your great strength lies, and what you might be bound to afflict you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Delilah asks openly how he "might be bound to afflict you." Arminian readers note that her intent is not hidden; Samson has every warning he needs and keeps choosing to stay, showing real responsibility for his downfall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the blindness of a man ensnared by desire. Scripture's wisdom literature warns of exactly this kind of folly, and Samson's story illustrates how sin dulls perception of obvious danger.

verses.text: Samson said to her, “If they bind me with seven green cords that were never dried, then shall I become weak, and be as another man.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samson's first answer is "seven green cords that were never dried." Arminian readers see him treating his consecration as a game, playing with the secret of a gift that belonged to God and not to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson lies to protect himself while staying close to the danger. His evasions show a heart divided, unwilling either to trust Delilah fully or to leave her as wisdom required.

verses.text: Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven green cords which had not been dried, and she bound him with them.
verses.arminianNotes: The lords supply the cords and Delilah binds him. Arminian readers note the coldness of her betrayal: she carries out the plan without hesitation, showing that her choices too were her own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Philistine lords are directly involved, bringing the materials themselves. The narrative makes clear that this is a coordinated attempt to destroy Israel's judge.

verses.text: Now she had an ambush waiting in the inner room. She said to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” He broke the cords as a flax thread is broken when it touches the fire. So his strength was not known.
verses.arminianNotes: With an ambush hidden in the inner room, Delilah cries, "The Philistines are on you, Samson!" He snaps the cords like thread. Arminian readers see Samson ignoring an unmistakable warning that she means to harm him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that God still upholds Samson's strength, and "his strength was not known." The repeated tests show God's patience toward his flawed servant even as Samson presses toward disaster.

verses.text: Delilah said to Samson, “Behold, you have mocked me, and told me lies. Now please tell me how you might be bound.”
verses.arminianNotes: Delilah accuses Samson of mocking her and lying. Arminian readers note the irony of her complaint, since she is the one plotting his capture, yet Samson keeps engaging rather than walking away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Delilah frames her betrayal as wounded love, a pattern of manipulation that wears Samson down. Sin often disguises its aims in the language of affection and grievance.

verses.text: He said to her, “If they only bind me with new ropes with which no work has been done, then I will become weak, and be as another man.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samson's second answer is "new ropes with which no work has been done," the same means Judah had used in 15:13. Arminian readers note that he keeps choosing deceit over honesty and danger over safety.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that new ropes had already failed in 15:14, when the Spirit came on him. The repeated detail shows that Samson's strength was never in the materials but in God's gift.

verses.text: So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them, then said to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” The ambush was waiting in the inner room. He broke them off his arms like a thread.
verses.arminianNotes: Delilah binds him with new ropes and again springs the ambush. Again he breaks free. Arminian readers note that each escape could have been a moment of repentance and departure, but Samson stays.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's restraint continuing. The narrative builds suspense while showing that God has not yet withdrawn his empowering, though Samson is drawing ever closer to the line.

verses.text: Delilah said to Samson, “Until now, you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me with what you might be bound.” He said to her, “If you weave the seven locks of my head with the fabric on the loom.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samson now mentions "the seven locks of my head," coming near the real secret. Arminian readers see a man drifting toward betrayal of his vow, each answer moving closer to the truth he was set apart to guard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson's hair was the sign of his Nazirite consecration (Numbers 6:5). By bringing it into the game, he moves from evasion toward treating his holy vow as a matter for play.

verses.text: She fastened it with the pin, and said to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” He awakened out of his sleep, and plucked away the pin of the beam and the fabric.
verses.arminianNotes: Delilah weaves his hair into the loom and fastens it with the pin; Samson wakes and tears it all away. Arminian readers note that he now sleeps while his consecration is being handled, a sign of dangerous complacency.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that even with his locks tied to the loom, his strength remains. God is still sustaining him, so Samson's later loss of strength comes not from the hair itself but from the LORD departing (verse 20).
